title: A 76-year-old reads a transient negative T-wave on his own Apple Watch ECG after gym exercise; work-up finds silent three-vessel disease and he has quadruple bypass surgery (Amsterdam UMC)
summary: Koster et al. (EHJ Case Reports, 30 Jan 2024): a patient-initiated lead-I watch ECG showed a negative T-wave normalizing after 22 min; exercise test, CT and angiography found 3-vessel disease; CABG.
account: Koster, de Winter, Verberne, Spijkerboer and Chamuleau of Amsterdam UMC reported in European Heart Journal Case Reports on 30 January 2024 (publication date used; the manuscript was received 26 June 2023 and the event is undated) a 76-year-old asymptomatic man with a strong family history of coronary disease, 30 years of treated hypercholesterolaemia and four years of type 2 diabetes who exercised weekly on a cross trainer and, very infrequently and 'solely out of interest', recorded a lead-I ECG with his Apple Watch immediately afterwards. On the last recording he noticed a negative T-wave that deepened over about seven minutes and returned to normal after 22 minutes, with no chest pain, breathlessness, dizziness or palpitations. He consulted a cardiologist; the resting ECG and examination were normal, but a bicycle exercise test two days later reproduced the lead-I T-wave change and showed ST depression up to 4 mm in V5. Cardiac CT showed stenoses in all coronary arteries (CAD-RADS 4), invasive angiography three-vessel disease, and a perfusion scan reversible ischemia in 16% of the myocardium. The heart team chose surgery and he received four bypass grafts; recovery was uneventful and a repeat exercise ECG at 11 weeks was normal. The authors note that Apple does not recommend the watch for detecting infarction or ischemia, that lead I is not ideal for ischemia, and that the finding requires systematic study before clinical use. The paper does not report any output from the ECG app's rhythm classifier; the abnormality was seen by the wearer on the trace and confirmed by clinicians.
purpose: The ECG app is built to record a single-lead ECG and classify atrial fibrillation; using the trace to spot exercise-induced ischemia is, as the authors say, not endorsed by Apple.
system: Apple Watch ECG app (single lead-I recording; its rhythm classifier is not mentioned in the report)
taxonomy_note: No health type exists; Accessibility chosen because a consumer device let the patient record an ECG minutes after exercise at a gym, which no clinical pathway would have captured in an asymptomatic man. The AI component of the ECG app (its atrial-fibrillation classifier) is not reported to have flagged anything, so this record documents a benefit from the device's recording function read by humans; the earlier verifier set it aside on that ground, and it is flagged for the owner's decision under the no-AI-involved rule.

ratings.reason: Silent, extensive, reversible ischemia from three-vessel disease was found and treated with quadruple bypass in an asymptomatic man; the authors' learning point is that such ischemia can end in exercise-induced sudden death, though the counterfactual is not established.

ai_role.statement: The watch recorded a 30-second lead-I trace at the wearer's initiative; the report gives no classification result from the app, and the negative T-wave was noticed by the patient and interpreted by cardiologists, who ordered the exercise test, imaging and surgery. No machine-learning output contributed to the finding as described. The single source is an independent peer-reviewed case report; no maker material was used.

produced_by: A wearer who records a watch ECG right after exercise and looks at the waveform, not only the rhythm label
A cardiologist willing to investigate a watch trace in an asymptomatic patient
Exercise testing, CT, angiography and perfusion imaging to confirm and grade the disease
must_hold: The lead-I trace reproduces T-wave changes faithfully, which the authors say appeared accurate though frequency characteristics are undocumented
Ischaemia that shows in lead I, which the authors call not ideal for the purpose
Tolerance of false positives and investigation cascades, which the authors flag as unstudied
